summary: Defines a format for e-mailing bibliographic records of technical reports, to speed the spread of information about new computer science technical reports. It was replaced by RFC 1807.

eli5.summary: A standard form for emailing library-card style details about new research papers, so everyone can list them the same way.

questions: how do you email technical report metadata
what fields are required in a bibliographic record
how do you withdraw a report
subtitle: A standard format for emailing metadata about technical reports

tldr.problem: Organizations announce new technical reports by mailing bibliographic records, which is costly, slow, and hard to archive electronically.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1357 defines a simple tagged text format for emailing bibliographic records that people and machines can create and parse without special software.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can share technical report announcements via email efficiently, and recipients can electronically file and search them. The format was later replaced by RFC 1807.

today: RFC 1807 replaced RFC 1357 as the standard for bibliographic record email format.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Computer science organizations traditionally mailed bibliographic records (library-card-style summaries) of new technical reports to announce them. This approach had two drawbacks: it cost money to print and mail, and recipients could not easily file or search the records electronically.

RFC 1357 proposes a simple tagged text format that organizations can email instead. The format is designed to be human-readable, machine-parseable, and creatable with any text editor. A tagged format means each piece of information (like title, author, or date) starts with a label followed by two colons, making it self-explanatory and easy to parse without specialized software.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing paper cards, send them by email in a simple plain-text format that both people and computers can understand.

sections.title: The Record Format
sections.content:
A bibliographic record is a single email message containing tagged fields. Three fields are mandatory: BIB-VERSION (which format version is used), ID (a unique identifier for the report), and ENTRY (the date the record was created). The record ends with an END field repeating the ID.

Optional fields include ORGANIZATION, TITLE, AUTHOR, DATE, PAGES, COPYRIGHT, RETRIEVAL information, and ABSTRACT. Fields can be repeated (for multiple authors) and can span multiple lines, with continuation lines indicated by starting with spaces. All text must be printable ASCII; tabs and special characters are forbidden.
sections.eli5: Each record is like a form with named boxes. You must fill in version, ID, and entry date. You can add optional boxes like title, author, and where to find it. Each box starts on a new line with its name and a colon.

sections.title: Fields and Uses
sections.content:
The BIB-VERSION field identifies the format version (currently CS-TR-v2.0). Experimental versions begin with X and should not be incorporated into permanent databases. The ID field has the format publisher-ID//report-number, where the publisher symbol is controlled to avoid conflicts and the report number is assigned by the publisher.

The DATE field records publication date (format: Month Day, Year or Month Year). The ABSTRACT field can hold up to 10,000 characters and should be included even if informal. RETRIEVAL fields describe how to obtain the full text, such as via FTP, mail, or email. Multiple RETRIEVAL fields can list different formats or access methods.

The CR-CATEGORY field references the Computer Reviews classification system. The REVISION field indicates updated records and carries a revision number and description.
sections.eli5: The ID is like a catalog number (who published it, plus its report number). The date follows a standard format. The abstract is a summary. Retrieval lines say how to get the full paper. If you fix an error, send a new revision.

sections.title: Example Record
sections.content:
The RFC provides a complete example record for a report titled The Computerization of Oceanview with High Speed Fiber Optics Communication from Oceanview University in Kansas. The record is about 1,750 characters long (220 words) and includes two authors, multiple retrieval options (postal mail and FTP), copyright information, funding sources, and a 40-word abstract.

Records can be revised by sending a new record with a higher revision number. A special form of revision withdraws a report by omitting the title and including an explanation in the NOTES field.
sections.eli5: Here is a real example showing all the pieces: who wrote it, when, how many pages, and how to get it. You can send an updated version if you made a mistake or change the retrieval info.
